en: Table of Contents for the *Luoxi Zhenzu Ji* (Anthology on the Revival of the Patriarchs at Luoxi): 1. Three Edicts Granted by Qian Zhongyi, King of Wuyue, to Dharma Master Jingguang; 2.
Inscription for the Stele Erected for the Chanjiao Yuan (Institute for the Transmission of the Teaching), bearing the Monastery Name bestowed under the Present Dynasty.
Epitaph for the Venerable Master Jingguang; Record of the Construction of the Stone Pagoda of King Yuga at Jianyuyuan Temple;
Epitaph for the Stupa of the Venerable Master Jingguang; Eulogy by Prime Minister Li Gong;
Eulogy by Prefect Zheng Gong; Verses by the Sangha Chief Tonghui.
*Gao Renwen De Dashi Shi*, *Chaan Fashi Zan*,
*Bateng Fashi Zan*, *Jingguang Fashi Yita Ji*,
and *Luoxi Zenzu Ji*.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Yuǎnwù, Abbot of the Tiāntái Chuánjiào Yùan.
The Imperial Edict (in three parts) bestowed by Qián Zhōngyì, King of Wúyuè, upon Dharma Master Jìngguāng.
Edict concerning the Monk Yìjì of Cānlín Temple, who, together with Dàshī Sīxuán and others, memorialized that they would lecture for the sake of the state at their own temple.
The *Fahua jing wenju shu* and other commentaries are all complete; they are indeed the product of refined virtue and exhaustive diligence.

As I perused them, I felt even greater admiration and gratitude. Therefore, I issue this decree for your information, which you should take note of. I have sent this letter; there is no need for further detail. The thirteenth day.

To the Venerable Sengyi Jiqing: You have long resided at a famous mountain, constantly studying the Great Canon. Our dynasty holds the True Teaching in high esteem and honors those of noble character.
We now bestow upon you the title of Master, along with purple robes and ten rolls of fine silk, as well as ten loads of cotton;
you may accept these. This decree is issued for your information; you should take note of it. No further details need be written. The twenty-ninth day.
Regarding the report submitted by Yi-je (義寂) concerning the recent assignment for you to preside over a single session of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* lecture at the Tianjie Monastery:

we have taken full note that the assembly has been successfully completed. We have long admired your reputation as a "Tiger of Vinaya" and a "Dragon of Meaning," and because you have already mastered the essence of consciousness and attained its fundamental source, we have commissioned you to propagate the Dharma. We have previously heard reports that you have already delivered lectures.

The announcement of completion upon chanting this [text] clearly demonstrates your refined cultivation; as you once again open and recite these precepts, I am deeply impressed by your diligent observance.
I now grant you twenty bolts of silk for medicinal milk and two hundred *jiao* of tea, which you may accept and take possession of. This message is sent for your information.
[Signature in Chinese seal]. Sent on the [day] of the ninth month.
Imperial Grant of a Title.
From the Imperial Yellow Edict of the Secretariat and Chancellery to the Circuit Intendant of the Two Zhe Provinces.

The Circuit Intendant of the Two Zhe Provinces memorializes the Central Secretariat, reporting on the analysis of the various prefectures, commanderies, and monasteries under his jurisdiction that were established during the illegitimate reigns, none of which have yet been granted official titles, as follows: [The list of establishments follows.]
Memorandum: It is hereby decreed that the Chuanjiao Monastery in Tiantai County, Taizhou, shall be granted the name “Dinghui Monastery.
In accordance with the preceding imperial edict, let the Transportation Commission issue this notification to all relevant locations and conduct a thorough and meticulous investigation.

If among them there are any [monasteries] that have already been granted names or titles on the occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday (Chengtian Festival), do not issue further notifications for them. This notification is issued in accordance with the imperial decree. Thus notified.
On the third day of the seventh month in the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era,
a notification was issued to Zhao [ ], Right Censor-in-Chief and Participant in State Affairs,
and Feng [ ], Vice Minister of the Ministry of War and Participant in State Affairs.
Epitaph for the Jianchuan Temple, composed by Wang Jian, Minister of Works and Chief Councilor; a meritorious official of loyalty,
sagacity, and heroic valor, serving as the Regional Inspector of the Jinzhou Commandery and Acting Minister of War.
Composed by Qian Yan, Grand Master of the Palace for Ceremonial Affairs, Special Advancement, Acting Grand Preceptor,
concurrently Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Upper Pillar State,
Duke of Pengcheng County with a fief of six thousand households and a real allotment of one thousand one hundred households, serving the state and military affairs.

The sages established written teachings by setting forth the fundamental principles and demonstrating the guiding tracks, so that people of later generations might reach the Way of the Sages and Worthies.

As for the matter of encompassing heaven and earth, exhausting yin and yang, fathoming good fortune and misfortune, and discerning waxing and waning—nothing is superior to the *Yi* (Book of Changes), which Fuxi initiated and Confucius expounded; thus it bestows enduring and sublime benefit upon the world.

The world is governed by means of the calendar, which binds the days to the months; it clarifies the past and examines the future, rectifying the Great Way and regulating human relations—nothing is more esteemed than the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
Confucius composed the canon, and Qiuming transmitted its commentary; this was to issue forth clear admonitions for ten thousand generations. May I venture to ask:

does the sage’s transmission of writings and establishment of teachings reach their ultimate point here? Little do we realize that he also transmitted the art of praise and censure through his writing.
If one cannot treat enemies and kin with equal impartiality, nor master the arts of investigating birth-and-death and the alternation of fortune and misfortune;

if one cannot fully express the wondrous nature and encompass the true mechanism—then as for being the ford and path for humans and devas, and crossing the deep abyss of birth and death, there is no teaching of the Great Hero (Mahāvīra) that is not vast and none that is not sacred.
As for the jade-like sounds being concealed on Vulture Peak and their transmission through the Dragon Treasury (Nāgārjuna’s collection):
As the precious scriptures grew increasingly distant from the Sage and were transmitted to posterity to provide enduring benefit,

there was none more magnificent than the teachings of Tiantai for expanding the waves of the fragrant ocean and strengthening the hubs of the Great Vehicle’s wheels. Thus, the National Master of the Chen and Sui dynasties,
the Great Master Zhizhe— whose Dharma name was Zhiyi— elucidated the grand purport of the Single Flower and established the flourishing school of the Eight Banners to clarify [the truth].

The sun of wisdom destroys the darkness and dispels the mists of ignorance to still the restless; the divine tortoise dances in the deep ocean as the four teachings—Distinction, Common, Separate, and Perfect—are revealed.
The five flavors of milk, cream, curd, butter, and ghee are transmitted in succession, proclaiming the light of Prajñāpāramitā.
The lamp illuminates the threshold of the Vaipulya gates, and like a long wind breaking through waves, the great mountain submerges the hosts of Māras within the gate of non-duality.
In Izumo, Shōshō expounded the True Dharma at San-no-uo, bequeathing it as a sublime scripture to propagate my true wind.

Consequently, kings and ministers turned their gazes toward the lecture halls of the Vermilion Hills, while cities, towns, and villages inclined their hearts toward the practice grounds of the Golden Land.
Thus, the transformation of people by Chizō was so vast in its benefit that it is beyond words to describe. — *Denkyō* (The Transmission of the Teaching)
The "Yuan" (Cloister) refers to the place currently presided over by the Great Master Jingguang, Master Ji. His dharma name is Yiji;
his secular surname is Hu, and he is a native of Yongjia. Previously, at the beginning of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, a resident of Luoxi named Zhang Yan'an came to the Master and said:
"To the southeast of my home, there is a vacant plot of land about one *li* in extent, which has been dark and gloomy..."
In the evenings, there were always sounds of ghosts and spirits wailing and howling, as well as the resonance of bells and stone chimes being struck.

Furthermore, he once dreamed that a divine dragon roamed this land; thus, it was not something that could belong to ignorant commoners. He wished to offer it to the Master for the sake of monastic affairs.
The Master accepted it and went in person to inspect it, sighing at the exquisite beauty of its mountains and waters. Thereupon, he said to the assembly: "This is a *gālaya* (monastery)."
Master Di constantly intended to perpetuate the True Vehicle and sought a place to preach and propagate it;
furthermore, since the Tian Tai school traces its lineage back to Nāgārjuna, could this not be the very sign of the divine dragon he had dreamed of?

However, as material offerings were not provided, he was unable to immediately fulfill his ambition, and thus accepted what was donated to cultivate a vegetable garden. Shortly thereafter, Master Fahua Yan...

The master’s disciple, Master Qi (whose name was Yuan; later he was also titled Chan Master Chongfa and was likewise a dharma-transmitting disciple of this master), reported these matters to his own teacher, the Chan Master.
The Chan Master greatly approved of the proposal and subsequently relinquished thirty thousand coins of alms he had received to provide the initial funds for the project.
Although the master rejoiced at such generous donations, he feared the heavy labor involved and thus cautioned Master Qi, saying: "Regarding what is now being undertaken..."
It was because he kept his disciples in mind, not wishing to shelter them from wind and rain by moving his household; rather, his intention was to fulfill his aspiration to dwell beneath a tree.
You should embody this intent and strive to bring it to completion. Thus, Master Qi excavated the mountain to establish the foundation and measured timber to raise the structures.

He built three bays for the Dharma Hall and several sheds for the kitchen; covering them with thatch and stacking them with mud, he adhered entirely to simplicity, following the heart of Master Yuecheng.
In the eighth month of autumn in the year of Gengdai Jiashi (940), when the hall was completed, he invited the Master to reside there.

The Master remained silent and subsequently led twenty disciples to go with him. At the nodding stone, they were arrayed against the verdant peaks; fresh flowers from the rain fluttered over the precious altar.
Furthermore, the Master beheld its rustic simplicity, which accorded with his desire for a peaceful dwelling; after settling there, he rejoiced.
Afterward, Wuliang ascended the halls of Yumen, where his daily offerings were overflowing; at Huque Garden, people suffered from the accumulation of robes.

When the Master heard of this, he discouraged such practices four or five times. However, the Chan Master Yunjushao, considering that the site of the *Lamp of the Dharma* had not yet been widely expanded and that the regulations for the master-disciple relationship (the "one-fathom" rule) were not yet established, drafted a memorial to the present King of Hannan, the Great Wise One.
The Master’s rank ascended through the various stages (*bhūmi*), his traces manifested as the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*); he attained the gate of *dhāraṇī* and acquired unimpeded eloquence.

The teachings he expounded fill several hundred fascicles; the Great Master Jingguang Yiji transmitted and lectured upon them, like water being divided among vessels (the above eight phrases are all recorded in the text of the aforementioned letter).

As for the hall and buildings of the monastery where he resided, they were not yet extensive; he requested permission to undertake their construction so that the pivot [of the Dharma] might find rest.

The King of the Assembly of Robes followed this advice and commanded his beloved sons, the two masters Xiang and Hua, as well as the members of the imperial clan, each to contribute money and grain to assist him.
Since the Master’s residence at Caotang was already exceptionally convenient and stable, he did not comply with the command for some time;
it was only in the fifth year, the year of Dingmao, that the construction was finally completed, including the reconstruction of the Hall of Repentance, the Dharma Hall, and the Meditation Chamber.
The scripture halls and auxiliary temple buildings were all fully prepared; from the interior to the exterior, there were over one hundred and thirty rooms in total.
Where the forest and springs shone upon one another, the golden and azure decorations were brilliantly radiant; wherever his flask and staff arrived, he forgot to return regardless of cold or heat.
In that year, the King again commanded the Master to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for a single session to perform meritorious services for the memory of the Queen Mother.
Lady Wu, the Senior Lady Yi, from this time forth, was like a divine dragon who rejoiced in hearing the Dharma, or a bird that delighted in the fragrance of offerings.
She partook of the pure food of Cunda, sat upon the seat of the Upoṣadha, leaned upon her armrest while grasping the whisk, and maintained a reverent and cautious mind.

The field of merit for the sea was clothed in robes, and the assembly gathered in great numbers. In the second year of the Taiping Xingguo era, Wang Junchengyi, the Commander-in-Chief’s Chief Officer of the Guard...
Internally, he learned that his guest, Mr. Yu Dehui, was deliberating with the court on the construction of a Maitreya Buddha Hall at the Institute.

The King further commanded the bestowal of eight hundred thousand coins and requested the Master to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* for one session, providing a vegetarian feast for thirty thousand monks.

Incense, flowers, banners, and canopies—all requisites for making offerings to the Buddha—were provided in full abundance. The following year, [the Master] presented his formal petition to attend the regular audiences.
The Great Sovereign of the Golden Wheel’s propagation of the Dharma flourished ever more, yet the adornment of sacred images remained incomplete, causing the hopes of the multitude to be stifled.
He therefore dispatched the monk Chongyun to the capital to request [the assistance of] Master Xiang.
Consequently, Master Xiang, together with Lady Xu of the Chen state and Xu Jue’an, the Gentleman of the Retinue of the Prince of Hanning, each donated two thousand coins.

One hundred thousand sets were fashioned with golden sashes; furthermore, the local official Li Congyu was recruited, and the multitude led him to contribute thirty thousand *jin* of pure wealth to complete the work.
Thus, the Peacock-Crested One and the Conch-Venerated One presided within the central throne, while the Lotus-Crowned One and the Leaf-Assistant supported the lofty platform.
With these, the majestic majesty of the retinue was established, and with them, the gentle grace of the attendants was realized; the profound golden mouths were deep and resonant.
His speechless brilliance was like that of a true talisman with its deep blue pupils; his gaze did not blink. Having perfected the Three Jewels, his hundred blessings were immeasurable.

Hearing that the Master’s wondrous conduct was profoundly cultivated, his compassionate heart was characterized by contentment: his clothing was but coarse cloth, his bed a single mat, and at the head of his staff hung only a water flask and a pouch.
Within his courtyard, he provided no bolts or locks. As he discoursed on the profound mysteries with tireless eloquence, fifty seats were never considered too many.
He has thoroughly mastered the Way of Joy, and his serene and flourishing presence within these three-tiered pavilions is not merely a matter of lofty transcendence.
Now, at sixty-eight years of secular age and forty-nine years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*), though his years are advanced, he remains tireless in instructing and guiding others;
he is truly a singular figure in the annals of the Sangha. Alas! As for the Tiantai teachings, they expound the meaning of the Unspoken Dharma of the Awakened King—how could they possibly omit this?

It clarifies that the source from which sentient beings take rebirth revolves in an endless cycle; thus, the three vehicles follow one another like chariots, gradually analyzing the provisional to enter the ultimate emptiness.
When the ten stages are grandly transcended, one then transforms the ordinary into the sagely. Why must one first point to a lotus upon the water to demonstrate the use of expedient means?
One should naturally awaken to the butterfly within a dream, realizing there is no separate essence. This is the meaning proclaimed here.

Who among them would not revere him as their patriarch and master? His disciples, the Grand Master Tongjian and Zhilian, honoring their teacher, established a Buddhist temple and opened a school for the Dharma.
Desiring to perpetuate his achievements through the long winter months, they requested that the carving of this inscription be undertaken.

However, I, Yan, reflect that on Mount Tiantai there have long been eminent scholars who have successively expounded the holy teachings; yet, as the pipes are difficult to play without mastery, one must first burn the inkstone [to erase one's errors].

Nevertheless, as I contemplate these verses and aspire to achieve the cause [of enlightenment], I venture to employ these flattering words to fulfill my wish: may the grassy enclosure be nourished by richness so that the roots of goodness are ever renewed;
may the wind from the Piḷamba grove stir the light of wisdom so that it never extinguishes. Thus, observing the fasts and precepts, I compose this inscription, which says:
[The inscription follows.]
When Fuxi passed away and Zhongni did not arise, how could your *Yijing* clarify the lines and images?
When Confucius died and Qiuming did not appear, why were the titles of your Lu annals lost?
The majestic True Teaching transcends birth and death; the vast and flowing Sanskrit sounds encompass both the provisional and the ultimate.
The crane-tree entered parinirvāṇa, its jade verses remaining secret; The conch-river ceased its discourse, so who shall now compile the flower-texts?
May the radiance of this analysis illuminate the various branches, And may the planting of the apricot and pine endure for ten thousand years.
The Epilogue says:
The peaks of Mount Tai rise majestically for several hundred fathoms; The Master of Teaching toils diligently to open the Jewel Forest.
Cold monkeys and wild cranes all contemplate the Dharma; From the lion throne, though silent, he proclaims the wondrous sound.
Written on the tenth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Yongxi era, the Bingxu year.
Epitaph for the Deeds of Master Jingguang,
composed by Qian Yi, Grand Master for Court Attendance, Acting Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, Compiler of Imperial Edicts,
and Recipient of the Purple Gold Fish Bag.

The mountains to the south of the capital are most extraordinary; those to the east, west, and north are high, deep, secluded, and remote. Thus, those who have renounced the world have taken up residence upon these terraces.

These terraces extend in all four directions for thousands of miles, and the mountains are further vast, hidden, and profound, such that they seem as though they could not be inhabited by ordinary humans.

In the past, our Master Zhi (the Wise One) sat upon this mountain to compose his writings; therefore, it became known as the Mountain of the Teaching of the Wise One (*Zhìzhě-shān*). Since the passing of the Master, [the tradition of] renunciation has continued here.
Those who have studied his teachings and grasped their essential meaning are found in great numbers. I heard this from Yue, where the account of the Master is most extraordinary.

The Master was of the Hu family of Wenzhou, Yongjia; for three generations his household had practiced the Buddhist scriptures. His mother, Lady Zheng, abstained from eating meat once she became pregnant with him.
When he was five or six years old, while playing with other children at the gate, he encountered three monks traveling in a carriage, fully equipped for a long journey.
On this road he encountered a group of children; one of them stroked the Master’s head and said, "You possess extraordinary destiny;

you shall become a preeminent figure within our school. After they departed, the Master looked back three times with an expression of longing. Later, he was further instructed in the Buddhist scriptures and worshipped the Buddha images as if performing no worldly human affairs.
At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order under Seng Zian of Wen to become a Buddhist monk.

The Master was diligent, prudent, clear-sighted, and sharp; he fulfilled the rites of a disciple to the utmost and was esteemed by his teacher, who transmitted to him the sutra known as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Within one month, he had completed its recitation. Whether rising, sitting, or resting, he possessed the dignified deportment of an ancient Buddha.
At the age of nineteen, he first shaved his hair and beard to become a bhikṣu. He then traveled to Yue to receive the Vinaya from the Vinaya Master Qing. III.
Having fully exhausted the ultimate path, he traveled south to Mount Tiantai to meet the Dharma Teacher Zhiyi, who was the successor to the masters Song and Guang.
First, he received the *Fahua benji buermen* (The Gate of the Non-duality of the Original and the Traced in the Lotus Sutra).

[He learned that] when the dharma-nature and ignorance universally produce all phenomena, it is termed "defilement"; when ignorance and the dharma-nature universally respond to various conditions, it is designated as the "pure cause."

Upon attaining sudden enlightenment to the Buddha-mind, his sweat fell like rain; within less than three months, he ascended the seat to preach extensively. He seated the two masters among the audience, feeling no shame whatsoever.

Whenever he entered the Tripitaka to select a single sutra, he never consulted commentaries or sub-commentaries, but lectured according to his own inspiration, causing all doubts to melt away like ice.
Soon thereafter, he expressed his intention to leave the mountain; those who had stopped there were all from the Tai region, yet none could [dissuade him].
During the Guangshun era, Yi Zhongyi’s uncle, who held the rank of Grand Marshal (Dàyuánshuài), was stationed at the capital in Xizhou when he heard of this;
he firmly urged him not to go elsewhere, granting him the Buddhist title of Jingguang Dashi (Master of Pure Radiance). After declining three times, he finally accepted the transmission.

He then established a Lotus Sūtra ritual arena (*dharmārambha*) and performed the Buddhist rites during the six periods of the day and night without slackening. In the autumn of the Jiǎzǐ year, he resided at Luoshan.
The affairs of the Xikang Monastery were like those of a formal ordination platform; my uncle, the Great Marshal, provided daily offerings there.

In the year of Dingmao, he retired from office and stayed at the East Tower of Kaiyuan Temple. As rain fell continuously for several days, one night he had a dream as if announcing that the tower was collapsing.

At dawn, he moved to another location. That same night, a great mountain collapsed and struck the tower, causing it to fall; nearly a hundred people were spared. This occurred during his early years in the Wu-Yue region.

After it had not rained for a long time, my uncle sent someone to seek out a master of prayer. The master led his disciples to a great pond, overturned their alms-bowls, and performed a ritual of invocation;
while they were chanting incantations in secret, after some time, the water in the pond was stirred by a wind, and suddenly something rose from within the water.
Before they had even returned halfway, a great rain fell continuously throughout the surrounding region, bringing relief to all. Furthermore, Xie Zu once sat in a meditative posture in his chamber.
There was a youth dressed in the garments of a mountain dweller, his physical form emaciated and haggard, carrying a bamboo vessel and nurturing small pine saplings with soil.
He knelt before the master’s chamber; the master inquired of him slowly, "Whence have you come? He replied, "I was sent from Mount Hōrin to deliver these pine seedlings.
Having finished speaking, he cast the bamboo vessel upon the ground and suddenly vanished. The master secretly said to his disciples, "This is a mountain deity."

"I shall dwell separately at the site of the Bodhimanda; this was the prior prophecy for the later founding of the Luoxi Teaching Institute. Generally, among the perilous sites south of the Way, Tiantai is foremost.
Below the Stone Bridge, the precipice overlooks ten thousand fathoms, with flying springs scattering in four directions; it is steep, slippery, and tilted, shaped like a transverse rainbow.
The Master once crossed it at night, where light preceded him like a row of torches, yet he cast his firebrands without anyone knowing their source.

Furthermore, when repairing the ruined image, many ancient artifacts were recovered; because there was a tally between them, it was determined that this image had been in the Imperial Secretariat as early as the sixth year of the Xiántóng era.

This was witnessed by the monk Xījiǎo, who made a vow at that time. [The image] has now been reborn here. Having entered the monastic order as a youth, he transmitted the Great Dharma and led the assembly;
they say he was the previous incarnation of the Master. As for the matter of Xǔ Yuándù serving the Master, it occurred in the past when [the Master] was in Sìmíng.
While staying at Yǔwáng Temple, I dreamed that I ascended to the upper story where there was a precious banner and a high seat with the words "Mañjuśrī Platform" inscribed in large characters.
Though the railings surrounded it, I could not enter; however, a Bodhisattva above reached out his hand to lead me by the hand, and I ascended with ease.
Upon awakening, my body and the Bodhisattva’s form were merged as one, indistinguishable. In the year Guǐwèi, the Emperor sent an official from within the palace...

The provincial officials and the prefectural governor entered the mountain to plan the construction of a Buddhist monastery and earnestly requested that the Master receive the Bodhisattva precepts, calling themselves his disciples.
Whenever the Master conferred the precepts upon people from the Tai region, there were those who gave up butchery to devote themselves to the study of sutras and śāstras;
those who abstained from eating meat; those who never spoke of killing until their death; and those who threw themselves from heights to die, making vows for rebirth.
There are those who abandon their wives and children to become followers of the Buddha (Futu), entering the mountains where they prostrate at every step until blood drips from their foreheads;
there are those who offer a hand or a finger as fire to the Buddha. Alas! When a great sound is raised once, its resonance echoes through a thousand valleys;
were it not for one who has ascended to such heights, who could penetrate the magnitude of these deeds? In the winter of the Dinghai year, the tenth month...
In the first month, he passed away from eye disease while lying on his right side; his spirit departed while his physical form remained upright and whole, as if he were still alive.
His disciples erected a shrine-casket in the quarters of the patriarchal hall, and the people’s grief was as if they had lost a close relative.

Five years later, when the burial site was moved, his body remained undecayed, emitting a pervasive and fragrant aroma. Is this not a sign of one who attained excellence within the Śākya teachings? The Master’s name was Yì.
Ji (寂) was sixty-nine years old [in secular age] and fifty years of *saṃgha* seniority (*śrāmaṇera-vassa*).

Previously, during the Taiping Xingguo era, an imperial edict appointed him as the Head Seat of the Left Street to preside over the Buddhist teachings in the Western Capital. Master Ning personally transmitted the biographies of eminent monks to him;

the Master’s conduct was such that it easily matched the accounts of former sages. Having long cherished a love for the good, he always desired to record extraordinary events with his brush to provide instruction, and thus he first became thoroughly acquainted with the Master’s life story.
Subsequently, I obtained another copy from my disciple Zhongxiu; upon collating and verifying it against the original, all points corresponded with the ancient text.
Is this not a case of having encountered a person of extraordinary character? At Zhongxiu’s repeated request, I composed an inscription for the Master’s stele.

Later, however, I declined out of deference, fearing that those fond of novelty might allow time to pass and cause the record to be lost. Therefore, I prostrate myself in reverence and respectfully compose these words.
The Inscription says:

The teaching is spread through the disciples, yet the disciples act as the masters of the teaching. When the disciples attain thorough understanding, it becomes ever more luminous; when the disciples are arrogant, they bring humiliation upon themselves.
Through luminosity, one accords with the Sage; through feeling, one follows the Truth. Arrogance leads only to fault; the fault does not lie in the corruption of the Teaching.

How great is our Master! He attained the Way and was in accord with the sages. Seated upon the high platform, he guided others; In his learning, he matched the ancient sages. While alive, his conduct was extraordinary;
Upon death, his remains were deemed miraculous. His fame resounded throughout the south, Causing his disciples to strive diligently in thought. Who are these disciples?
They are those who can perfect their observance, Wearing it upon them for all time, Without falling into falsehood or blame.
Record of the Newly Constructed Stone Stupa of Yūwang at the Denpō-in, composed and calligraphed by the temple disciple (Nikkyō).

The World-Hero’s [Śākyamuni’s] work for the sake of sentient beings has come to rest; he has concealed his form within the secret treasury, and only the stupa and image remain. Some have sealed them with jade and silk cords...
The golden bones stand as a towering banner, such that every turn of the head or raising of a hand becomes a wondrous occasion; this is not accidental.
There was a venerable monk named Shoucheng who, for many years, had cultivated *dhyāna* within and performed meritorious deeds for the Buddha externally.

Regarding all matters of virtuous benefit, there was nothing he did not know how to do. One day, he arrived with a gracious air, and when the subject of this magnificent site was raised, he remarked that it was truly extraordinary.
"Nothing can rival the enduring solidity of the sacred stupas of the Sage; there is nothing that surpasses the eternal fame of inscribed stone.

I, though ignorant, have joined forces with others to cultivate this great merit. Having heard of this, how could I dare not offer praise? Thus, we collectively solicited contributions from both monastics and laypeople, obtaining over sixty thousand coins in loans.
We then commissioned stone artisans to complete four structures, and within less than a year, the work was fully accomplished. Of these, two were raised five *gao* high."

First, it was established in the courtyard of the monastery; subsequently, it was placed in the Samantabhadra Repentance Hall. These were chosen as the most auspicious sites, each being perfectly suited for its purpose.
Its physical form was modeled after the Mahāsthūpa of King Aśoka, cast from various precious materials without any omission or deficiency.

Within it was enshrined the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the sublime discourse from Vulture Peak; therefore, there was no need to further install relics, for it was said that [the Sūtra] itself already contained the Tathāgata.
This is the arrival of the entire body; how much more so when one takes the true mark (*dharmatā*) as the Way, for which there is no distinction between gold and stone, or the vast and the minute.

Even if the kalpa-fire burns the void and the blue wind shakes the earth, how could it destroy it? Being ignorant, I do not presume to write these clumsy words here, yet I have recorded them directly.
Recorded on the eighth day of the eighth month in the year of Dayuanyuan (875), during the eighth year of the Kaibao era of the Great Song.
The Epitaph for the Stupa of Master Jingguang, composed by his disciple [Cheng or].

The Master’s name was Xiji, his style name was Changzhao; he was of the Hu family and a native of Yongjia. He received the tonsure and entered the monastic order at the [Kai]feng Temple in his own prefecture.
At the age of nineteen, Yuan Si received full ordination and studied the Vinaya at Kuaiji. He subsequently relied upon Guoqing Monastery to study the Tiantai teachings.
From the time of Master Zhizhe until Master Zhanran, the lineage had been transmitted from lamp to lamp, spreading throughout the world.

Although the subtle words were briefly defiled and the transmission temporarily suspended during the destruction by Emperor Wuzong of the Tang, Yuan Si was able to apply himself with diligent effort to their contemplation and flavor, propagating them everywhere.

He composed texts for the civil service examinations and instructed others without weariness. Having resided in the mountains for forty-five years, he guided more than two hundred students in his learning.
During the reigns of the Deng, Wang, and Qian dynasties, they revered his virtue and morality;

they bestowed upon him purple robes and a monastic title, constructed dwellings to provide him with peace, and provided offerings to sustain him. Today, throughout the provinces and prefectures, those who transform and propagate the teachings are many of his disciples.
The Master conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon approximately several hundred thousand people; his virtuous deeds and life history are recorded in full in the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha).

On the fourth day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Yongxi era, the cyclical year being Dinghai, he passed away in his chamber at the age of sixty-nine, with fifty years having elapsed since his ordination.
The following year marked the commencement of the Endong era, the cyclical year being Wuzi; on the sixteenth day of the final month of summer, [the funeral rites were performed].
A stupa and pavilion were erected at the southeastern corner of Guoqing Monastery for his interment. Among his more than twenty disciples, the eldest was Lingyu;
those who carried on his legacy were Jiaoruru and Shikeli. They served him according to ritual and buried him according to ritual.
If this is so, what cause for regret is there in the literary record? This fool, having the misfortune of inheriting the later flame, has thoroughly studied the traces of the past. Thus...
It is said: The wise one’s perfect teaching follows the footsteps of former masters; prodigious men have appeared in successive generations. His virtue is as warm as jade;
he labors tirelessly to promote the Dharma and instructs others with meticulous care. He raises the sail upon the ocean of the Law and holds aloft the candle in the dark alleys of ignorance.
Where does the sounding staff shake? The stupa is sealed within a deep valley. Dharma-sons and Dharma-grandsons continue the lineage like one lamp lighting another.
In the "Praise for Master Jingguang," Li Shen, Minister of the Palace Secretariat and Director of the Chancellery, and Xu Ling [state]:
"Master Yi: The Way honors the worthy. Li Su, Master Ran: "Diligence consists in constant attendance."
The two disciples were fortunate to hear the teachings proclaimed by the two masters; they sprinkled the nourishing dew of wisdom and purified the lotuses of their hearts.
My Master Jingguang’s fragrant reputation remains: in non-explanation and non-demonstration, he attained the profound mystery.
His form was solemn within his chamber, yet his transformation flowed beyond the heavens; though the terrace of Tiantai did not move, his pure influence has continued unceasingly.
Eulogy by Master Jingguang for Zheng Yuangui, Court Gentleman of the Third Rank, Acting Left Reminder, and Acting Military Governor of Taizhou:
Like clouds, ever-shifting; The luster of pearls from Hepu; The brilliance of jade from Kunlun.

It is fortunate to hear that the teachings of the Zhìzhě have been restored. As the chanting of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* resounds day and night beyond the lecture hall, the sound and rhythm are like those at Nánshān where the Way is practiced; surely spirits and deities must be supporting him from beneath his feet.
(The Master and his disciples constantly recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the sound of the scripture never ceasing day or night).
Dharma Master Chān (Yǒuyán) offered this praise:

"Without considering my own incompetence, I have come to expound these magnificent teachings. My traces are lodged within the purple palace [of the monastery], yet my heart is moved by the utmost virtue; having beheld [the Master], I am filled with reverence."
This portrait remains here; how could I not dare to offer these humble verses in praise? Alas! I humbly pray that you will look upon me with your enlightened discernment.
I recall in the past, when the mists of ten thousand *li* were cleared away, a single star of virtue shone brightly over the Southern Terrace.
The name of the Cultivator of Truth first arose from the Divine Land; those who admire the Dharma and become monks come mostly from Japan.
The mechanism of the Way was nearly becoming a great pest; The lamp of wisdom was successively reduced to cold ashes.
Had there not been the supporting power at that time, The vastness of kalpas of dust would have been a matter for lamentation.

Dharma Master Jingguang was truly a patriarch who revived the lineage of the Teaching and Contemplation (Jiaoguan). His stupa stood amidst mountain ravines where mud and water had long seeped in, leaving it overgrown with brambles and fallen into neglect.
Now, the current abbot Yuanwu has relocated it to a more open and elevated site and constructed a pavilion to enshrine it.
This serves as the main chamber for the abbot’s quarters. To initiate the restoration of such ruins must indeed have been a difficult undertaking. As for Dharma Master Jingguang: [text continues].

The legacy of his virtue and the praises of former masters must not fail to be widely propagated; I therefore continue the preceding rhyme, though I beg you not to reproach me for my reckless and unrefined composition.
I, the Dharma-grandson (Shanyue), residing abbot of the Tianzhu Linggan Guanyin Jiao Temple, prostrate myself with my head at your feet.
The traces within the patriarchal blessings reveal an opening; The lofty pagoda reflects the light of the Three Terraces.
As the teaching flows to the lands across the sea, its origins are traced back; The blue-dyed lineage has its own long-standing tradition.
Precepts are as pure as the deep, clear bottom of a pearl; The Way participates in the profound realization, and the Vinaya disperses like flying ash.
A thousand years later, Luoxi is but a trace of the past; the Dharma-gate is worthy of both sighs and lamentations.
The record of the relocation of the stupa at Luoxi:
To die and be buried is ancient; to bury [the deceased] immediately is not ancient. That it is not ancient yet involves immediate burial is perhaps a matter of expedient means (*upāya*).
Is it for the sake of accomplishing the task? In ancient times, the former kings held that burial is concealment; concealment means desiring that others not see [the remains].

Therefore, they provided coffins and outer cases, shrouds and linings to lift [the body], divined the location of the grave site to settle [the deceased] there in peace—thus there was the practice of burial.
After the Venerable Luoxi had passed away, his disciples enshrined his entire body...
To the southeast of Zangguo Temple, following secular rites, this has been so for over two hundred years.
As the years have passed, the waters have lost their ancient course, causing obstructions, submergence, and subsidence, leading those who walk its paths to sigh in lamentation.

Yuanwu, having mistakenly assumed these duties, surveyed the flow of the springs and observed the yin and yang energies; he found a suitable site behind the Abbot’s quarters in the tenth month of the Jiayin year of the Shaoding era.

In the fourth day of the first month, the burial was moved and a stone stupa was erected there. Now, the practice of covering exposed bones and burying remains is intended for those who have not yet attained realization.
When the Venerable One was alive, he regarded this body as already identical to an illusory transformation; now that he has passed away, the truth of his single nature is present everywhere.
What harm is there in being near water? Furthermore, why would one need to move it? Nevertheless, for the sake of the students...
With such profound faith and utmost reflection, I have experienced a sense of fragrant warmth and solemn sorrow as if I were actually seeing him;
for were it not so, there would be no way to secure the intent of honoring one’s master and revering the Way, nor to perpetuate its lineage for eternity.

As for investigating the origins and details of the transmission, recording the entirety of his virtuous conduct, and chronicling the auspicious signs of spiritual resonance, these matters are already documented in the historical records.
The lineage record remains extant.
On the first day of the full moon in the first month of the Xinmao year of the Shaoding era of the Sacred Song Dynasty, the dharma-grandson bhikṣu (Yuǎnwù), the current incumbent,
bows his head to the ground in reverence and records this.
